## Where Week 2 sits

This week turns a chosen finite representation $K$ into chain vector spaces,
boundary maps and homology. The purpose of the construction is understanding:
we want to see exactly how a visible loop becomes an algebraic class, and why
filling that loop changes the answer.


[Lecture walkthrough](solutions.ipynb)

---

## Simplices are filled building blocks

| $p$ | $p$-simplex | vertices |
|---:|---|---:|
| 0 | vertex | 1 |
| 1 | edge | 2 |
| 2 | filled triangle | 3 |
| 3 | filled tetrahedron | 4 |

An outline triangle is three edges. It is not a 2-simplex until its face is
included.

---

## Read the house as a complex

![](../../assets/week02-house-complex.svg){fig-alt="A labelled house complex with five vertices, six edges and one filled roof face." height="290"}

- $K_0$: vertices $A,B,C,D,E$;
- $K_1$: edges $x,y,z,u,v,w$;
- $K_2$: filled roof $t=[A,B,E]$.

The room interior is absent. The roof interior is present.

---

## Downward closure

$$\sigma\in K,\ \varnothing\ne\tau\subseteq\sigma
\Longrightarrow\tau\in K.$$

If the roof $[A,B,E]$ is present, its three edges and three vertices must also
be present.

**Counterexample.** A hypergraph may record a four-player football team
$\{A,B,C,D\}$ without asserting every pairwise relationship. That is a valid
hyperedge, but it is not a 3-simplex in a simplicial complex.

---

## Chains in the house

$$C_1=\operatorname{span}\{x,y,z,u,v,w\}.$$

A chain is any algebraic selection of edges:

$$y+u \quad\text{is valid even though it is disconnected.}$$

Two useful chains are

$$r=x+v+w\quad\text{(roof)},\qquad
q=y+z+u+w\quad\text{(room)}.$$

---

## Boundaries in the house

$$\partial_1y=B+C,\qquad \partial_2t=x+v+w=r.$$

For the room outline,

$$
\partial_1q=(B+C)+(C+D)+(D+E)+(E+B)=0.
$$

Every vertex occurs twice and cancels over $\mathbb F_2$.

The roof outline also has zero boundary, but it is itself the boundary of the
filled roof.

---

## The chain complex

$$
\cdots\to C_2(K;\mathbb F_2)
\xrightarrow{\partial_2}C_1(K;\mathbb F_2)
\xrightarrow{\partial_1}C_0(K;\mathbb F_2)\to0
$$

$$\partial_{p-1}\partial_p=0.$$

Therefore

$$B_p=\operatorname{im}\partial_{p+1}\subseteq
Z_p=\ker\partial_p.$$

---

## Algebra survival kit

Kernel: inputs sent to zero.

Image: outputs the map can produce.

Quotient: identify differences we agree to ignore.

[Open the pre-Week 2 algebra guide](algebra-survival-guide.qmd)

## What $Z_p/B_p$ means

$$z\sim z'\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z-z'\in B_p.$$

Two cycles represent the same class when the region between them is an available boundary.

One class, many representatives.

---

## Examples

### Same 1-skeleton, different complex

![](../../assets/week02-outline-filled.svg){fig-alt="Outline and filled triangle with the same 1-skeleton but different first homology." height="225"}

Outline triangle:

$$C_2=0,\qquad z=e_{01}+e_{12}+e_{02}\in Z_1\setminus B_1.$$

Filled triangle:

$$C_2=\langle [012]\rangle,\qquad z=\partial_2[012]\in B_1.$$

The cycle remains. Its class in $Z_1/B_1$ changes.

::: {.sticking}
**▶ Likely sticking point.** A simplicial complex is not determined by
its drawing or its 1-skeleton. The triangular 2-simplex is extra data.
:::

---

## Boundary maps become matrices

Choose simplex bases and fix their order. Each column of $[\partial_p]$ is the
boundary of one $p$-simplex.

Over $\mathbb F_2$:

$$[\partial_{p-1}][\partial_p]=0,
\qquad
\beta_p=\dim C_p-\operatorname{rank}\partial_p-
\operatorname{rank}\partial_{p+1}.$$

::: {.object-check}
**◇ Object check.** The matrix is a representation of a linear map. Its
rows and columns only make sense after the chain-space bases are named.
:::

---

## A richer worked example: the house

![](../../assets/week02-house-complex.svg){fig-alt="A labelled house complex with one filled triangular roof and one unfilled square room." height="245"}

The filled roof cycle is a boundary. The square room cycle is not.

$$
H_0\cong\mathbb F_2,\qquad
H_1\cong\mathbb F_2,\qquad
H_2=0.
$$

The [Week 2 notes](index.qmd#cycles-boundaries-and-homology-in-the-house)
derive this from the complete boundary matrices.

---

## Examples to compute

Use a square loop as the simplest visible $H_1$ class and a hollow
tetrahedron as a first $H_2$ example. Ask explicitly which chains are
cycles, which cycles are boundaries, and which distinctions survive in
the quotient.

---

## A graph is not its clique complex

Same vertices. Same edges. Different complex.

Graph alone: the triangle is an $H_1$ cycle.

Clique complex: the triangular 2-simplex fills that cycle.

Clique filling asserts that mutual pairwise interaction represents a coherent
higher-order unit. That is a modelling choice.

---

## Two computational checks

$$\beta_p=\dim C_p-\operatorname{rank}\partial_p-
\operatorname{rank}\partial_{p+1}.$$

$$\chi(K)=\sum_p(-1)^p\dim C_p
=\sum_p(-1)^p\beta_p.$$

Euler characteristic is a check, not a replacement for homology.
